CISA KEV: CVE-2026-50751 — Check Point Security Gateway Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-08 6 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

Check Point Security Gateway contains an improper authentication vulnerability in IKEv1 key exchange that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass user authentication and establish a remote access VPN connection without a valid user password. Vendor: Check Point, Product: Security Gateway. Known ransomware use: Known. Federal patch due: 2026-06-11.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-50752")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-50752")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Node-gyp Supply Chain Compromise: A Self-Propagating npm Worm That Hides in binding.gyp

Snyk
2026-06-04 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A new npm worm is abusing binding.gyp to trigger node-gyp during install, letting malicious packages run code without lifecycle scripts. It steals credentials, persists in GitHub, and self-propagates across maintainers.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Miasma/Node-gyp loader file hashes present on developer or CI host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Phantom Gyp: node-gyp install-time code execution via weaponized binding.gyp · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Node-gyp Supply Chain Compromise: A Self-Propagating npm Worm That Hides in bind
Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phantom Gyp: node-gyp install-time code execution via weaponized binding.gyp AIExploitation High
Hunts the Miasma/Phantom Gyp install-time execution primitive where a malicious binding.gyp uses gyp command substitution (<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)) to run node index.js during npm install with no preinstall/postinstall hook. Anchors on the exact, byte-identical shell string shipped in @vapi-ai/server-sdk@1.2.2 and autotel@3.4.3. Rationale: Anchors on the byte-for-byte 157-byte binding.gyp payload string '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)' quoted verbatim in the Snyk write-up and confirmed by StepSecurity's 'Phantom Gyp' analysis — the 'echo stub.c' + 'index.js' pairing has no benign equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://socprime.com/active-threats/miasma-supply-chain-attack-spreads-through-the-phantom-gyp-worm/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/binding-gyp-supply-chain-attack-compromises-dozens-of-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate native addon whose binding.gyp coincidentally runs a helper named index.js (rare; would not also echo stub.c)
  • Internal build tooling that pipes a node script to /dev/null during CI configure steps
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • Developer testing a custom gyp command-expansion build step
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has "node-sass" or ChildCmd has "\\test\\fixtures\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd; confirm the parent chain is npm/node-gyp and the command contains both 'index.js' and 'echo stub.c'. Identify the package directory under node_modules and the package@version. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, kill the node process tree, and treat any npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault/Kubernetes credential reachable from that context as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the Bun download (UC2), .github/workflows injection (UC3), and the loader hashes (UC4); enumerate other hosts that installed the affected package versions via lockfiles.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "index.js" and ProcessCommandLine has "stub.c"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "echo stub.c" or (ProcessCommandLine has "/dev/null" and ProcessCommandLine has "index.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "index.js" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "stub.c"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "echo stub.c" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/dev/null"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma loader fetches standalone Bun v1.3.13 from oven-sh GitHub releases during install AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma second-stage loader that, after binding.gyp triggers index.js, downloads a standalone Bun v1.3.13 binary from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases via curl and unzips it to a temp dir to run the next stage. Anchors on the hardcoded release URL path. Rationale: The Snyk decode of the 907-byte first decrypted blob quotes the literal URL template 'https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/bun-<os>-<a>.zip'; the pinned 'bun-v1.3.13' release path inside a curl/install context is a high-fidelity, low-noise anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://socprime.com/active-threats/miasma-supply-chain-attack-spreads-through-the-phantom-gyp-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately installing Bun v1.3.13 via curl for a real project
  • CI pipeline that provisions Bun as a build dependency
  • Dockerfile build step pulling that exact Bun release
  • Mirror/proxy cache warmers fetching the oven-sh release artifact
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker.exe","dockerd","buildkitd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process is node/npm (not an interactive shell or Dockerfile RUN) and check whether index.js / binding.gyp execution (UC1) preceded it on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, block egress to the temp-dir Bun binary, kill the process tree, and rotate all reachable cloud/CI credentials. 3) Hunt: inspect the temp directory for the unzipped bun binary, look for subsequent credential-file reads (~/.npmrc, ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud, kube config, Vault tokens) and outbound GitHub API calls used for exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma GitHub Actions workflow injection for persistence by node payload AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Miasma worm injecting GitHub Actions workflow files (.github/workflows/*.yml) for persistence, written by a node/npm process rather than a developer's editor. Targets the persistence step that lets the worm re-trigger and re-exfiltrate from CI. Rationale: The article and StepSecurity both state the worm 'injects GitHub Actions workflows for persistence'; constraining the writer to node/npm/bun (the install-time payload host) separates worm injection from a developer authoring workflows in an editor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://cybersecuritynews.com/binding-gyp-supply-chain-attack-compromises-dozens-of-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A scaffolding tool (e.g. a generator run via node) legitimately creating .github/workflows during project init
  • Yeoman/create-* CLIs writing CI templates
  • A node-based codemod that rewrites workflow files in bulk
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation editing workflows locally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "create-" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "yo "
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written workflow yaml — look for steps that exfiltrate env/secrets, curl to attacker GitHub repos, or re-run the install payload; correlate with UC1/UC2 on the same host. 2) Contain: revert/remove the injected workflow, revoke the repo's Actions tokens and any GITHUB_TOKEN/PAT, and rotate cloud secrets stored as Actions secrets. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos the compromised maintainer account can push to for the same injected workflow, and review recent npm publish events from that account.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "\\.github\\workflows\\" or FolderPath has "/.github/workflows/"
| where FileName endswith ".yml" or FileName endswith ".yaml"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/.github/workflows/" or TargetFilePath has "\\.github\\workflows\\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("yml","yaml")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","bun")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma/Node-gyp loader file hashes present on developer or CI host AIDelivery Medium
Alerts on any of the seven published Miasma loader SHA256 (and SHA1) hashes appearing as a written or executed file on endpoints/CI runners. Direct IOC match for the obfuscated index.js loader chain from the Node-gyp Supply Chain Compromise - June 2026. Rationale: Uses the seven SHA256 and three SHA1 hashes pre-extracted from the article (the Miasma loader chain); a direct hash hit is unambiguous TP and requires no behavioral inference. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox host intentionally storing the sample for analysis
  • SOAR enrichment that downloads the IOC file for sandboxing
  • Backup/AV quarantine copy of the same file re-hashed on a second host
  • Hash collision (negligible for SHA256)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the file path and the npm package@version it belongs to (node_modules/...); confirm whether it was merely written or also executed (correlate with UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, delete/quarantine the file, and rotate every credential reachable from that host (npm, GitHub, AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault, Kubernetes). 3) Hunt: pivot on the package versions named in the Snyk advisory (@vapi-ai/server-sdk 0.11.1/0.11.2/1.2.1/1.2.2, ai-sdk-ollama, autotel 2.26.4/3.4.3, awaitly 1.33.3) across all lockfiles and CI caches in the estate.
let badSha256 = dynamic(["ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90","5926b86b642e00672252953eb30d8f75cfb7797fe3118bd6fa2cfbee92905d61","ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1","82d83274680df928fdda296a348e01802f595e412308c399565c320df444052a","288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a"]);
let badSha1 = dynamic(["8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6","608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686","ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ (badSha256) or SHA1 in~ (badSha1)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let badSha256 = dynamic(["ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90","5926b86b642e00672252953eb30d8f75cfb7797fe3118bd6fa2cfbee92905d61","ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1","82d83274680df928fdda296a348e01802f595e412308c399565c320df444052a","288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (badSha256)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents

Type Level Security: The future of secure AI code generation?

Snyk
2026-06-04 1 use case 1 technique 1 kill-chain phase detected

Secure-by-design types can turn common bugs into compile-time errors. This post explores how type-level security could help prevent entire classes of AI-generated vulnerabilities.

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Package manager runtime connecting to durabletask/axios supply-chain C2 IOCs AICommand & Control High
Network connections from node/python/npm/pip processes to the C2 IPs and domains attributed to the March 2026 axios npm hijack and May 2026 durabletask Python backdoor. Pivots on the article's exact infrastructure observables so it survives binary renaming and code refactors. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact C2 IPs (142.11.206.73, 160.119.64.3) and domains (sfrclak.com, check.git-service.com, t.m-kosche.com, packages.npm.org typosquat of packages.npmjs.org). Initiating process scoping to node/python/npm/pip turns this from a flat IOC sweep into a supply-chain-specific signal that distinguishes the malicious-package-postinstall pattern from a workstation browsing.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package mirror reverse-proxied through the same IP range (rare; verify by ASN)
  • Security researcher sandbox replaying IOCs against test hosts
  • Misconfigured npm config pointing to packages.npm.org typo unrelated to the campaign
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline that resolves the IOCs for enrichment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\InternalMirror\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alerting host — what package (npm/pip) installation kicked off the node/python that egressed? Confirm whether the host is a dev workstation or CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response; rotate any cloud credentials (AWS/Azure/GCP/K8s/Vault) sourced from that host in the last 14 days; quarantine the offending package version from the internal registry. 3) Hunt: search Defender DeviceNetworkEvents and DNS logs across the org for the same IPs/domains over 30 days; pivot on the parent package name in npm/pip audit logs to enumerate every host that installed it; review CloudTrail/AzureActivity for AssumeRole/STS or kubectl exec from those hosts.
let MalIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","160.119.64.3"]);
let MalDomains = dynamic(["sfrclak.com","check.git-service.com","t.m-kosche.com","packages.npm.org"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where RemoteIP in (MalIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (MalDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let MalIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","160.119.64.3"]);
let MalDomains = dynamic(["sfrclak.com","check.git-service.com","t.m-kosche.com","packages.npm.org"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr in (MalIPs) or DstHostname has_any (MalDomains) or Url has_any (MalDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Lateral movement via aws ssm send-command or kubectl exec spawned by python/node AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the durabletask post-compromise tradecraft — backdoored Python (or its node equivalent) shelling out to aws/kubectl to spread laterally using the victim's own credentials via SSM SendCommand/StartSession or kubectl exec. The parent-runtime pivot is what makes this article-specific rather than a generic admin-tool detection. Rationale: The article specifies the durabletask backdoor spread 'to other instances over SSM and to other pods via kubectl exec' using the victim's own credentials. Filtering AWS/kubectl execution to a python/node parent makes this an actual supply-chain signal rather than admin-tool noise, and the CloudTrail variant catches the same activity by user-agent footprint when EDR isn't on the host.
ATT&CKT1021.007 T1609 T1078.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python-based CI orchestrator (Ansible, custom build scripts) legitimately running aws ssm send-command against fleet
  • Boto3-driven SSM automation for patch management
  • Kubernetes operators (written in Python/Go served by node) routinely exec'ing into pods
  • Developer using Boto3 in a Jupyter notebook to debug SSM run-commands
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","\\salt\\","\\jenkins\\","\\gha-runner\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating package — pull npm/pip install history and DeviceProcessEvents for the python/node parent's full ancestry; confirm the package matches durabletask or a known-bad supply-chain release. 2) Contain: revoke the IAM role / kubeconfig the runtime used (rotate STS, invalidate kubeconfig tokens); isolate the host; snapshot to forensic storage before reboot. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail for every SSM SendCommand / StartSession originating from the compromised role across the org window; enumerate target instances and pull EDR on each; in K8s, audit kube-apiserver logs for exec verbs from the same ServiceAccount and walk the affected pods.

Downloader or shell child of npm/pip install (postinstall RAT loader) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the axios-style postinstall pattern where a malicious package's install hook reaches out for a second-stage payload via curl/wget/powershell/bitsadmin. The parent-equals-package-manager pivot turns generic downloader behavior into a supply-chain-specific signal. Rationale: The axios hijack 'added one new dependency whose only job was a postinstall script that pulled down a cross-platform RAT and deleted itself' — the loader behaviour is a download from a non-language-runtime binary spawned by the package manager. Parent==package-manager + child==downloader + URL/download-cmdline is the article's exact shape.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / native-module build pulling source archives via curl during install
  • Python wheels with C extensions running curl to download CMake/MSBuild prerequisites
  • pnpm/yarn fetching tarballs from a private registry that resolves through curl-based postinstall scripts
  • Corporate npm proxy doing legitimate token fetches via PowerShell
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","cmake-js"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full process tree (npm/pip → downloader → ?) and the downloaded URL; query the org for every host that installed the same package@version. 2) Contain: quarantine the package version in the internal registry; pull the host offline; revoke any tokens that touched the registry. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for files written by the downloaded process within ±10 minutes of the alert; pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for any subsequent connections; enumerate other developer machines that ran the same package install over the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","pip3","yarn","pnpm")
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash","sh","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-OutFile","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pip","pip3","node","python","python3","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","powershell","pwsh","bitsadmin","certutil","bash","sh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-OutFile","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud credential file access by node/python runtime AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the durabletask second-stage credential harvest where a backdoored Python (or node) runtime reads .aws/credentials, .azure, .kube/config, gcloud config, .vault-token, and .npmrc. Targets the file paths the article enumerates — AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Vault. Rationale: The article states the durabletask second stage 'harvested credentials from AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, and Vault'. The standard paths for those credential stores (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, ~/.azure, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.vault-token, ~/.npmrc) being touched by node/python is the concrete behaviour. The runtime filter keeps this from firing on AWS CLI / kubectl / az themselves.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Boto3-based deploy scripts legitimately reading ~/.aws/credentials for SDK auth
  • Python K8s client (kubernetes-client) loading ~/.kube/config on startup
  • Pulumi/CDK programs written in Python/TypeScript reading multi-cloud creds during deploy
  • Azure SDK for Python loading cached ~/.azure tokens
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws-sdk","boto3-sts-refresh","pulumi","cdk deploy","kubernetes-client"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the parent of the node/python process — was it spawned by npm/pip install? Identify the package; pull the file's hash and check VirusTotal/threat intel. 2) Contain: rotate every cloud credential touched (AWS access keys, Azure refresh tokens, GCP service-account keys, Vault tokens, npm publish tokens); revoke kubeconfig context tokens; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/AzureActivity/GCP audit for use of those credentials from new IPs in the last 14 days; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the host's outbound connections after the file access to identify exfil destination; pivot on the package name across the org install logs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any (@".aws\credentials", ".aws/credentials", @".kube\config", ".kube/config", @".azure\", "/.azure/", "/.config/gcloud/", @"\gcloud\", ".vault-token", ".npmrc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@".aws\credentials", ".aws/credentials", @".kube\config", ".kube/config", @".azure\", "/.azure/", "/.config/gcloud/", @"\gcloud\", ".vault-token", ".npmrc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Locale-conditional rm -rf wiper command from python/node runtime AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the durabletask wiper logic — a one-in-six destructive rm -rf /* invoked from a Python/Node interpreter on hosts with Israeli or Iranian locale. The rm -rf /* + python/node parent combination is the article's exact tradecraft. Rationale: The article states: 'On hosts with Israeli or Iranian locale settings, a one-in-six roll ran rm -rf /*'. The parent==python/node + cmdline==`rm -rf /*` combination is the literal article-specific impact behavior — extremely high signal because a developer never legitimately wipes their own root.
ATT&CKT1485 T1561.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Docker container init script that legitimately runs `rm -rf /tmp/*` during cleanup (regex anchored to root prevents this)
  • Dockerfile build steps spawned from a Python orchestrator that include destructive cleanup of build artifacts
  • Test harness for filesystem code that intentionally invokes the command in a sandbox
  • Misconfigured CI cleanup job using --no-preserve-root for non-root directory wipes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker build","buildx","kaniko","Dockerfile"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is critical — page the on-call analyst immediately. Confirm whether the command executed successfully (check for filesystem damage, host responsiveness). Identify the package that introduced the python/node parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host and any peers that received SSM/kubectl exec from it; snapshot the disk for forensics before any restore; quarantine the package version across the registry. 3) Hunt: search the org for every host that installed the same package@version and any process tree containing the rm command; pull locale settings (LANG/LC_*) from those hosts to identify which were targeted; check for the article's IOCs (142.11.206.73, 160.119.64.3, sfrclak.com) on the same hosts to confirm campaign attribution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","python","python3","node")
| where FileName in~ ("rm","sh","bash","busybox","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brm\s+-rf\s+(/\*?|--no-preserve-root)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brm\s+-rf\s+(/\*?|--no-preserve-root)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,

        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

StepSecurity
2026-06-02 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Several packages in the @redhat-cloud-services npm scope were found to carry malicious payloads that fire via a preinstall hook on every npm install. The affected versions span multiple packages across the RedHat Cloud Services frontend ecosystem. The payload is a sophisticated multi-stage credential harvester that targets GitHub Actions secrets, AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, HashiCorp Vault, npm tokens, and CircleCI tokens

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Bun runtime download to /tmp from a node process during npm install · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Multiple redhat-cloud-services npm Packages compromised
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm preinstall hook executing oversized node index.js from @redhat-cloud-services package · [LLM] Bun spawned from npm install context executing /tmp/p*.js implant
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Process reading /proc/<pid>/mem of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (in-memory secret extraction)
npm preinstall hook executing oversized node index.js from @redhat-cloud-services package AIInstallation High
Detects the entry point of the @redhat-cloud-services supply-chain compromise: a preinstall script firing node against an unusually large (>1 MB) index.js shipped inside an @redhat-cloud-services scoped package directory. The legitimate libraries in this scope have tiny entry files, so a 4.2 MB index.js executing during install is a near-deterministic signal of the malicious version. Rationale: Anchors on the exact preinstall execution string named in package.json (`node index.js`) combined with the scoped-package path `@redhat-cloud-services` and the article's distinguishing 4.2 MB size of index.js (vs <100 KB for legitimate releases). Cross-checked against the StepSecurity disclosure and the three RedHatInsights GitHub issues (#492, #2329, #57). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/RedHatInsights/javascript-clients/issues/492 • https://github.com/RedHatInsights/frontend-components/issues/2329 • https://github.com/RedHatInsights/platform-frontend-ai-toolkit/issues/57
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RedHat dev tooling installs on engineer workstations once a clean version is republished — pin to the known-malicious versions in the affected-packages table
  • Internal mirrors that proxy the registry may still serve a cached malicious tarball after upstream removal
  • Security-team-controlled detonation sandboxes installing the bad versions intentionally for IR
  • CI re-runs from cached node_modules tarballs that pre-date the cleanup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--ignore-scripts") or ProcessCommandLine has "--ignore-scripts")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the installed package@version against the affected-packages table (e.g. host-inventory-client@5.0.3, types@3.6.1); pull the on-disk index.js size and SHA256; correlate with the GitHub Actions run / developer workstation identity. Step 2 — Contain: kill the node process; quarantine the host's node_modules; rotate every secret the host had access to (AWS, GCP, Azure, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, Vault, CircleCI, Kubernetes kubeconfigs); revoke OIDC-issued tokens minted during the window. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on UC2/UC3/UC4 for the same host; search registry-mirror access logs for the malicious versions being pulled by other workloads; review GitHub branch-protection bypass and any commits signed by the same OIDC identity during the install window.
let SuspectPackages = dynamic(["@redhat-cloud-services/types","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-utilities","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components","@redhat-cloud-services/rbac-client","@redhat-cloud-services/javascript-clients-shared","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-config-utilities","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-notifications","@redhat-cloud-services/tsc-transform-imports","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-config","@redhat-cloud-services/eslint-config-redhat-cloud-services","@redhat-cloud-services/host-inventory-client","@redhat-cloud-services/rule-components","@redhat-cloud-services/notifications-client","@redhat-cloud-services/chrome","@redhat-cloud-services/hcc-pf-mcp"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","node","node.exe","yarn","pnpm","npx","npm-cli.js")
| where FileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@redhat-cloud-services" and ProcessCommandLine has "index.js"
| extend MatchedPackage = tostring(set_difference(SuspectPackages, dynamic([])))
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FolderPath has "@redhat-cloud-services" and FileName =~ "index.js"
    | where FileSize > 1048576
    | summarize MaxSize = max(FileSize) by DeviceId, FolderPath
) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MaxSize, MatchedPackage
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectScope = "@redhat-cloud-services";
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Facility in ("user","daemon","kern") or ProcessName in ("auditd","audispd")
| where SyslogMessage has "node" and SyslogMessage has SuspectScope and SyslogMessage has "index.js"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm-cli.js","npx","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 4f8a3c2d-9e1b-4a7c-8f60-1b9d2e3c4a51
description: Detects node executing an index.js inside a @redhat-cloud-services scoped package directory during npm install, the entry point of the June-2026 supply-chain compromise.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/multiple-redhat-cloud-services-npm-packages-compromised
author: SOC Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/01
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  parent_selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/npm'
      - '/node'
      - '/yarn'
      - '/pnpm'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
  child_selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '\node.exe'
  cmdline_selection:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '@redhat-cloud-services'
      - 'index.js'
  condition: parent_selection and child_selection and cmdline_selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*node*@redhat-cloud-services*index.js* OR *Node*@redhat-cloud-services*index.js*) AND (@process.parent.name:(npm OR node OR yarn OR pnpm OR npx) OR @process.command_line:(*preinstall* OR *"npm install"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/(node|node\.exe)$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|npx)(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("@redhat-cloud-services", field=CommandLine)
| regex("index\\.js", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

Bun runtime download to /tmp from a node process during npm install AIDelivery High
Detects Stage 3 of the redhat-cloud-services compromise: the in-memory _b downloader retrieves bun-v1.3.13 from the official Bun GitHub releases CDN and drops it into a randomly-named /tmp/ subdirectory, then registers it via globalThis.getBunPath. Article-specific because legitimate library installs never fetch a parallel JS runtime at install time. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact runtime version `bun-v1.3.13`, the GitHub releases CDN host (`objects.githubusercontent.com` is the actual blob host behind github.com release downloads), and the `/tmp/<random>/bun` drop path described in Stage 3. Pairs network event with the file-create within 5 minutes to suppress generic Bun installs on developer machines. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/tag/bun-v1.3.13
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually running curl/bun installer to try Bun on a workstation
  • CI image-build steps that legitimately download Bun for a project that uses it (rare in RHEL/insights tooling)
  • Renovate/Dependabot autodeps tasks that exercise package install in sandboxes
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a previously-cached corrupt Bun binary
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("package.json\"bun\"","bunfig.toml") or DeviceName has_any ("-bunlab-","-bunci-"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the parent of the node download is an npm install of an @redhat-cloud-services package; capture the URL, the dropped /tmp/<random>/bun, and its SHA256. Step 2 — Contain: kill node, the Bun process, and any /tmp/p*.js it spawned; isolate the host; revoke any cloud / GitHub OIDC tokens issued to the runner. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to UC3 (/proc/<pid>/mem reads by Bun) and UC4 (Bun executing /tmp/p*.js); look across the fleet for any other host that fetched bun-v1.3.13 from a node process — every hit is a likely-compromised CI runner.
let BunDownload = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","npm")
    | where (RemoteUrl has "github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases" or RemoteUrl has "bun-v1.3.13" or RemoteUrl has "objects.githubusercontent.com")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
let BunDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
    | where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or FolderPath startswith "/var/folders/"
    | where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","tar","unzip")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
BunDownload
| join kind=inner BunDrop on DeviceId
| where Timestamp1 between (Timestamp .. Timestamp + 5m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, DropPath = strcat(FolderPath, FileName), InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunNet = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where (Url has "github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases" or Url has "bun-v1.3.13" or DstHostname has "objects.githubusercontent.com")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm")
    | project NetTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url, DstIpAddr;
let BunDrop = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EventType == "FileCreated"
    | where TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/folders/"
    | where TargetFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
    | project DropTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName;
BunNet
| join kind=inner BunDrop on DvcHostname
| where DropTime between (NetTime .. NetTime + 5m)
| project NetTime, DropTime, DvcHostname, Url, DstIpAddr, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by NetTime desc
source:linux.auditd ((@process.name:(node OR npm) AND @network.destination.domain:(*github.com OR *githubusercontent.com) AND @process.command_line:(*bun-v1.3.13* OR *oven-sh/bun*)) OR (@auditd.type:PATH AND @file.path:(/tmp/*/bun OR /tmp/*/bun.exe) AND @process.name:node))
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^(github\.com|objects\.githubusercontent\.com)$/i ContextImageFileName=/\/(node|npm)$/i)
OR
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^\/(tmp|var\/folders)\/[^\/]+\/bun(\.exe)?$/i ContextImageFileName=/\/(node|npm|tar|unzip)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, DomainName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port values(All_Traffic.user) as user values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node","node.exe","npm") (All_Traffic.url="*github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases*" OR All_Traffic.url="*bun-v1.3.13*" OR All_Traffic.dest="objects.githubusercontent.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | join type=left src [| tstats summariesonly=false values(Filesystem.file_path) as bun_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/*" (Filesystem.file_name="bun" OR Filesystem.file_name="bun.exe") by Filesystem.dest | rename Filesystem.dest as src] | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Process reading /proc/<pid>/mem of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (in-memory secret extraction) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the credential-harvesting core of the implant: reading /proc/<pid>/mem of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process to scrape secrets that the runner holds in memory but never writes to disk. This is exactly the activity the StepSecurity Harden-Runner screenshot in the article captured and is the technique the payload uses to evade Harden-Runner-style detections by reading rather than calling out. Rationale: Anchors on /proc/<pid>/mem — the exact /proc read the article's Harden-Runner process-events screenshot captures — combined with node/bun as the reader (the Stage 1 entry point and the Stage 3 downloaded runtime). Joins forward to DeviceProcessEvents on the target PID to confirm it is Runner.Worker, eliminating debugger / strace noise. Source: StepSecurity blog + image SCR-20260601-oxms.png in-article screenshot showing Runner.Worker /proc/mem read. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/007/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/multiple-redhat-cloud-services-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based debugger or profiler legitimately attached to a worker for performance work
  • Systemd-coredump or abrt-hook-ccpp reading process memory during a crash dump (different parent, usually root-owned)
  • Custom observability agent written in node that reads /proc to monitor RSS (verify by image hash / installed-package source)
  • SRE running strace -p / gdb -p against the runner during incident response
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gdb","strace","perf record","abrt-hook-ccpp","systemd-coredump") or AccountName == "root" and InitiatingProcessFileName == "systemd-coredump")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent tree of the node/bun reader; confirm the target PID is Runner.Worker by joining to process-create events; capture /tmp/<random>/bun SHA256. Step 2 — Contain: kill the node and bun processes; isolate the runner; revoke the runner's GitHub Actions OIDC tokens and every workflow secret the job had access to (GITHUB_TOKEN, AWS_*, GCP_*, AZURE_*, NPM_TOKEN, VAULT_TOKEN, CIRCLE_TOKEN, KUBECONFIG); rotate any long-lived keys downstream actions chained to. Step 3 — Hunt: search the fleet for any other process reading /proc/<pid>/mem of Runner.Worker (different package may share the same TTP); review last 30 days of GitHub Actions secret usage from those workflows; audit all artifacts produced by jobs that ran this implant.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileOpened","FileAccessed","FileCreated")
| where FolderPath startswith "/proc/" and FileName == "mem"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","bun")
| extend TargetPid = extract(@"/proc/(\d+)/", 1, FolderPath)
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FileName has_any ("Runner.Worker","Runner.Listener")
    | project DeviceId, TargetPid = tostring(ProcessId), RunnerCmd = ProcessCommandLine, RunnerName = FileName
) on DeviceId, TargetPid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, TargetPid, RunnerName, RunnerCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let ProcMemRe = @"/proc/\d+/mem";
let RunnerHits = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where SyslogMessage matches regex ProcMemRe
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("node", "bun")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage;
let AsimHits = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where TargetFilePath matches regex ProcMemRe
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "bun")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath;
union isfuzzy=true RunnerHits, AsimHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
